questions.question_text: Cylinder P has a radius of $4$ cm and a height of $18$ cm. Cylinder Q has a radius of $6$ cm and a height of $9$ cm. In exact form in terms of $\pi$, by how much is the larger volume greater than the smaller?

options.why: Subtracted the squared radii and the heights separately, evaluating $\pi(36-16)(18-9)$.
Doubled the difference, as though each cylinder had two circular ends to count.
Added the two volumes together instead of subtracting to find the difference.

questions.solution_text:
Cylinder P: $V = \pi \times 4^{2} \times 18$
$= 288\pi\text{ cm}^{3}$
Cylinder Q: $V = \pi \times 6^{2} \times 9$
$= 324\pi\text{ cm}^{3}$
$324\pi - 288\pi = 36\pi\text{ cm}^{3}$

questions.question_text: The radius of a cylinder is doubled and its height is left unchanged. The volume of the new cylinder is how many times the volume of the original?

options.why: Assumed the volume grows by the same factor as the radius, ignoring the square in $\pi r^{2}h$.
Cubed the scale factor instead of squaring it, as though the height doubled as well.
Applied the factor of $4$ to the height as well as to the circular cross-section.

questions.solution_text:
Original: $V = \pi r^{2}h$
New radius $2r$: $V = \pi(2r)^{2}h$
$= 4\pi r^{2}h$
The new volume is $4$ times the original.
